answer.rationale: Only two memories have recovered source records this cycle, and they diverge sharply in reliability. memory_86 is confirmed by exp_86 (completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%) — it is the single direction with verified evidence of BOTH acquisition-side and retention-side benefit, which is exactly what 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' requires. memory_73, by contrast, is a lossy consolidation: the archived source exp_73 shows signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% but 30-day retention -12%, with an explicit source-level instruction not to generalize targeted discounting as sustainable growth. The consolidated memory silently dropped the retention harm and the do-not-generalize warning. Matching the competitor's price cut is therefore the option the memory layer makes look most attractive and that the underlying evidence most clearly forbids — it would buy signups from a cohort that does not survive first renewal, worsening the very churn pressure leadership is reacting to. This discovered consolidation failure is a downstream value risk that generalizes: memory_31, memory_57, memory_91, and memory_44 are all still-unverified consolidations of the same pipeline, each stated as a clean positive with no counter-evidence recorded — precisely the shape memory_73 had before its source was recovered. I am therefore not treating them as decision-grade, and I am queuing all four for verification next week when archive access returns. Given the verification budget is spent, I run the onboarding improvement at standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout: exp_86 was validated on self-serve accounts, while the acute pressure is on price-sensitive SMB accounts already in churn conversations, so the population transfer is an untested assumption. A measured rollout with retention instrumentation lets us respond today without overclaiming external validity, and shortening time-to-value is a defensible non-price answer to a price attack because it raises realized value rather than lowering the price of unrealized value. Recommend leadership be told explicitly that price-matching was considered and rejected on evidence, not omitted.
